source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? (Who&When, full PDF read)
finding: Gap 8. Three ways to read a failure log: all-at-once, step-by-step, binary search. All-at-once is best at naming the agent, step-by-step best at naming the step. Binary search sits in the middle and costs about twice all-at-once. Accuracy falls as logs get longer.
numbers: Hand-crafted systems, GPT-4o, no extra reasoning prompt: all-at-once 17,106 tokens, agent 57.02%, step 4.39%; binary search 34,659 tokens, 43.97% / 6.90%; step-by-step 87,720 tokens, 35.96% / 7.90%. With a tolerance of 5 steps all three reach about 33-37%. Context levels run from 5-17 steps to 93-130 steps; at the longest level all three methods trend toward near 0%.
limits: Bisection does not fix step-level accuracy; it trades agent accuracy for a small step gain. One benchmark, mostly GPT-4o; the hand-crafted set is small.
agent_relevance: For S5 on a long log: do not read it whole and do not bisect blind. Narrow the responsible part first, then scan steps in that part. Allow a tolerance window when scoring.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Who&When: hybrid method and reasoning-model table
finding: Gap 8. Coarse-to-fine hybrid: all-at-once picks the agent, then step-by-step scans only that agent's steps. This beats any single method on step accuracy but costs the most tokens. Strong reasoning models do not rescue step-level accuracy.
numbers: Hybrid: 149,177 tokens, agent 57.02%, step 12.28% (vs 4.39% all-at-once, 7.90% step-by-step). Table 4 step-level: all-at-once 4.39 (GPT-4o), 10.34 (o1), 3.45 (R1); step-by-step 7.90, 13.79, 6.90. Removing the explicit-reasoning prompt cut step accuracy by 7.4% (all-at-once) and 4.4% (step-by-step).
limits: Hand-crafted subset only for the hybrid; small sample; no variance reported.
agent_relevance: Coarse-then-fine localization works for logs too, but costs about 9x the tokens of the cheapest method. Spend it only when the first coarse pass is uncertain.

source: West et al. (2025) Abduct, Act, Predict: Scaffolding Causal Inference for Failure Attribution (A2P)
finding: Gap 8. A three-step scaffold (abduct the cause, act by designing a fix, predict the outcome) lifts step-level failure attribution by a large factor over the Who&When baselines.
numbers: Algorithm-Generated: 47.46% step accuracy vs 16.67% baseline (2.85x). Hand-Crafted: 29.31% vs 12.07% (2.43x). Baselines reported below 17% step-level.
limits: Abstract only read. Same benchmark as Who&When. The gain comes from a counterfactual check (predict what a fix would do).
agent_relevance: A counterfactual step (if I change this step, does the failure go away?) is a cheap scaffold-only way to raise localization accuracy. Fits S5.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AgenTracer: Who Is Inducing Failure in LLM Agentic Systems?
finding: Gap 8. A trained 8B tracer beats big prompted models at failure attribution and improves agent systems when its feedback is used.
numbers: Prompted reasoning LLMs below 10% on the task (abstract). AgenTracer-8B beats Gemini-2.5-Pro and Claude-4-Sonnet by up to 18.18% on Who&When. Feeding its feedback back gave 4.8-14.2% gains on MetaGPT and MaAS.
limits: Abstract only. Needs training, so outside our no-training rule; useful as an upper bound.
agent_relevance: Shows the ceiling for prompting alone is low; the scaffold has to supply structure the model lacks.

source: Guo et al. (2026) BLADE: Auditing Information Use for Failure Attribution
finding: Gap 8. Controlling which parts of the log the judge sees gives small but steady step-level gains over all-at-once across eight strategies.
numbers: 1,228 failed runs over five subsets of Who&When and Who&When Pro; best or tied-best step accuracy; +2.2 to +11.1 percentage points over All-at-once.
limits: Abstract only; models not named; single-lab preprint.
agent_relevance: What evidence enters the context matters as much as which model reads it.

source: Error-Propagation Modeling for Failure Attribution (EMFA) (2026)
finding: Gap 8. Modelling how an early error spreads to later steps raises step accuracy.
numbers: +3.45 points (Hand-Crafted) and +4.40 points (Algorithm-Generated) over the previous best on Who&When.
limits: Abstract only; absolute accuracies not in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Look for the earliest step whose error explains later errors, not the most visible one.

source: Hou et al. (2026) EDGE: Error Dependency Graph-Guided Multi-Error Attribution
finding: Gap 10 (partial). Real traces often hold several errors. An error dependency graph helps category-level multi-error attribution on TRAIL and MAST. The abstract gives no numbers.
numbers: No figures in the abstract. Claims gains across most evaluated models and settings (EMNLP 2026 listing).
limits: Only qualitative evidence read. Multi-error is attributed at category level, not tested inside a repair loop.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping more than one candidate fault alive. No direct test of single-fault breakage in repair loops was found.

source: Listing of 2026 failure-attribution preprints (DCFA, DuoTrace, ASCon, CockpitHAT, Trial by Trace)
finding: Gap 8. At least 113 arXiv papers match failure attribution in agents by Nov 2026. Snippet gains: DCFA up to +8.27% step-level; DuoTrace +7.7%; ASCon +10.63% micro-accuracy; CockpitHAT step-exact 37.8/46.0/38.2% (listing says withdrawn).
numbers: As listed in snippets. Gains are relative to differing baselines.
limits: Only search-result snippets read, not the papers. Do not cite these numbers as verified.
agent_relevance: The field moves fast; step-level attribution is still the weak spot, so keep the scaffold's step claims hedged.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts (UoT), NeurIPS 2024 (PDF read)
finding: Gap 1 and 9. Planning the next question by simulating answers and scoring expected information gain beats direct prompting on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and troubleshooting. Gains are largest when the candidate set is closed and given.
numbers: Average success-rate gain 38.1% (relative to direct prompting, 5 datasets, 5 LLMs). Troubleshooting (FloDial) GPT-4 closed-set: 43.7% to 67.3%, mean successful length 7.8. Llama3-70B closed-set DX 83.7 to 90.4; MedDG 60.2 to 64.3. Open-set Llama3-70B MedDG 25.7 to 50.6. Beats CoT-SC by 33.8% and Reflexion by 29.9%.
limits: Simulated answerer (an LLM playing the user, no wrong answers tested); toy diagnosis tasks; no equal-token comparison; not real software faults. Gains are relative figures.
agent_relevance: Supports picking the next probe by expected information, but only on closed candidate sets with a reliable answerer. Not proof on real bugs.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM, ICLR 2026 (PDF read)
finding: Gap 1 and 9. Real expected information gain, with the LLM as a likelihood model, beats asking the LLM for a good question, and beats plain entropy, on 20 Questions. Asking the LLM to pick the most informative of several candidate questions still beats plain prompting, cheaply.
numbers: Average +37.4 percentage points success rate over direct prompting; more than doubled in over half the setups; never decreased. Entropy-only is the strongest alternative and slightly beats the halving (Split) baseline.
limits: Toy tasks (20 Questions, film preferences); the answerer is an LLM. Authors note entropy alone fails when answers are noisy even given the hypothesis, which is the noisy-oracle issue of gap 2.
agent_relevance: Use expected information gain over entropy when the check can be noisy; a cheap fallback is to have the model rank candidate probes.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: hierarchical localization ablation (PDF read)
finding: Gap 7. A three-step coarse-to-fine localization (file, then class/function skeleton, then edit lines) is more accurate and cheaper than jumping to lines or dumping whole files. An LLM does reproduce block-level search.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite (300 issues). File level: prompting alone 78.7%, embedding alone 67.7%, combined 81.7% contain the true file. Related elements: complete file 53.67% at $0.15, skeleton 58.33% at $0.02 (context 778 vs 698 lines). Going directly from file to edit lines is worse and costlier than via related elements. Final: 96 fixes (32.00%), average $0.70.
limits: One benchmark; the paper's own ablations; the benchmark has known leak and weak-spec issues (see b14).
agent_relevance: Block-level first, then cell-level: confirmed as token-saving for LLM localization. Use skeleton views, not full context.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: patch validation ablation (PDF read)
finding: Gap 3 and 6. Test-based gates are what lift correct fixes among many candidates. Majority vote alone gives 77; adding regression tests 81; adding model-generated reproduction tests 96, at $0.25 more.
numbers: Majority voting 77 (25.67%), $0.00; plus regression tests 81 (27.00%), $0.01; plus reproduction tests 96 (32.00%), $0.25. Upper bound if the best patch were always picked: 126 (42.0%). Plateau at about 40 samples.
limits: Reproduction tests are written by the same LLM; see d13 for their error rate.
agent_relevance: The cheapest strong gate is an executable check that the fault is gone plus a check that nothing else broke. Voting alone is weak.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: quality of LLM-written reproduction tests (PDF read)
finding: Gap 2 and 6. LLM-written checks are often wrong. Of 213 reproduction tests that reproduced the issue, only 94 also passed after the true fix (44%).
numbers: 300 problems; 213 tests reproduce the issue; 94 verify the ground-truth patch (44.1%).
limits: This is a verifier of fixes, not a human oracle. Mitigated by requiring regression tests first.
agent_relevance: An agent's own check can be wrong far more than 10-25% of the time. Treat its verdict as soft evidence and combine it with an independent regression check.

source: Wang and Hong (2025) Time Travel: LLM-assisted semantic behavior localization with git bisect
finding: Gap 8 and 2. Putting an LLM judge inside classic bisection, with step-wise reasoning meant for noisy commit judgments, lifts success and cuts bisect time.
numbers: Success rate 74.2 to 80.6 percent (+6.4 points); up to 2x lower average bisect time; several open source projects; a fine-tuned DeepSeekCoderV2 was used.
limits: Abstract only; baseline unnamed; involves fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: Bisection with a noisy judge is workable if the judge reasons per step.

source: Ulfat et al. (2026) Measuring LLM Trust Allocation Across Conflicting Software Artifacts (TRACE)
finding: Gap 2 and 6. When docs, code and tests disagree, LLMs catch faults in text far better than in code behaviour, and their confidence barely separates right from wrong.
numbers: 22,339 valid responses, 7 LLMs, 456 Java method bundles. Doc faults caught 67-94%; doc-implementation contradictions 50-91%; detection drops 21-43 points when only the implementation changes; confidence separates correct from incorrect poorly for 6 of 7 models.
limits: Injected faults; abstract only; models unnamed.
agent_relevance: Do not let the agent trust prose over executed behaviour. Weigh evidence by source type.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Gap 6. Verbalized confidence is overconfident. Sampling consistency and better aggregation reduce this, but no method wins everywhere and expert-knowledge tasks stay hard.
numbers: 5 models, 5 dataset types. White-box over black-box edge is small: AUROC 0.522 to 0.605.
limits: Abstract only; not debugging tasks.
agent_relevance: Do not use stated confidence alone to decide when to re-open S5; combine consistency and a check.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: Gap 6. For RLHF models, verbalized confidence is better calibrated than token probabilities.
numbers: About 50% relative cut in expected calibration error (abstract).
limits: Abstract only; QA tasks not debugging.
agent_relevance: Verbalized confidence is a cheap signal, yet d16 shows it still overshoots; use both with a check.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? Survey
finding: Gap 3. Survey of self-correction. The abstract reports no figures; its message is that gains need reliable external feedback or fine-tuning.
numbers: Abstract contains no figures.
limits: Abstract only; the stated conclusion is from the survey's framing as read in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Supports gating revision on an external signal, matching b15 and d12.

source: Chen et al. (2022) CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests
finding: Gap 6 and 3. Letting the model generate tests and choosing code by agreement with those tests beats picking by the model alone.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 65.8%, +18.8% absolute over code-davinci-002; 4 benchmarks, 5 models.
limits: Abstract only; function-level generation, not repair.
agent_relevance: Earlier evidence that model-made tests can gate model-made code, in line with d12 and d13.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Gap 2 and 3. Models do worse when a task unfolds over several turns than when given in one go.
numbers: Average 39% performance drop across six generation tasks; over 200,000 simulated conversations.
limits: Abstract only; generation, not diagnosis.
agent_relevance: A probe-and-answer loop is itself a risk. Keep each revision turn anchored to all evidence so far.

source: Joshi et al. (2023) FLAME: a small language model for spreadsheet formulas
finding: Gap 5. A 60M-parameter model trained on formulas beats much larger models at formula repair and completion in 10 of 14 settings. No tracing or dependency-graph tool is used; the lift is from domain training.
numbers: 60M parameters vs Codex 175B and 12B and CodeT5 220M; two orders of magnitude less training data; 10 of 14 evaluation settings.
limits: Abstract only. Not about error-value (#REF!, #NUM!) cases specifically.
agent_relevance: Does not answer gap 5. Shows formula-specific signals can matter more than size.

source: Ma et al. (2024) SpreadsheetBench: abstract re-check
finding: Gap 5. The benchmark has 912 real forum questions and a substantial gap to human performance. The abstract has no figure for error-value tasks, so that gap stays open.
numbers: 912 questions; no accuracy numbers in the abstract.
limits: Per-category results need the full paper.
agent_relevance: Do not claim any tool-use effect on error-value spreadsheets without a source.

source: Chopra et al. (2024) Exploring Interaction Patterns for Debugging with AI assistants
finding: Gap 1. A user study of conversational debugging with insert-expansion (assistant asks a clarifying question mid-task) reports a 5x gain in bug resolution.
numbers: 12 industry professionals, within-subjects; 5x improvement in bug resolution rates (abstract).
limits: Abstract only; small N; not information-gain based; the 5x basis is not stated in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Real-developer evidence that asking before answering may help, with no equal-token control.
